title: From Plant to Patients: Functional and Structural Traits of Plant Pyrroline-5-Carboxylate Synthetase (P5CS) Allow Experimental Deciphering P5CS Mutation-Associated Human Diseases
content: Pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthetase (P5CS), a bifunctional single-chain filament-forming enzyme, catalyzes the first two steps of proline biosynthesis, a crucial process in humans. Its mutations cause two recessive and two dominant genetic syndromes representing a mutation-specific pathologic continuum proposed to reflect enzyme deficiency of varying magnitude, where dominant mutations would act by negative dominance mechanisms. We support here these tenets by studying enzyme activity and stability for twenty-one mutant forms of plant P5CS (AtP5CS2: much more favorable for functional studies than human P5CS) which recapitulate the P5CS disease spectrum, also using single-particle electron microscopy (EM) with selected mutations. Recessive mutations caused enzyme deficiency, in most cases because of misfolding. As demanded by dominant negative mechanisms, dominant mutations yielded well-folded protein with different degrees of dysfunctionality or diminished stability. Negative-staining and cryo EM confirmed filament formation by wild-type AtP5CS2, while negative-staining EM proved that three of the five dominant mutations prevented such filamentation, without always abolishing enzyme activity. These observations exclude for P5CS activity the generally assumed need of filament-based channeling of the unstable intermediate L-glutamyl-5-phosphate. Our work sheds novel insight on the P5CS mutation-associated disease spectrum and exemplifies the value of plant biotechnology for human pathology.
